I'm the OP and am going to "weigh in" to better explain why I'm personally conflicted about this issue. I've always felt that obesity was nearly exactly the same as cigarette smoking--both voluntary vices (some would say addictions) that are extremely unhealthy. The government spent 20-30 YEARS trying to educate the public into the health-risks of smoking, but usage stats remained high. It took an outright campaign of public shaming, forcing smokers outside into the cold, and levying massive taxes before the tide turned and smoking rates began to drop.

I honestly believe it might take 20-30 years before we get beyond this HAES bullshit and the government finally starts taking the obesity epidemic seriously. But I ask myself "what will it take?" Shitlords like us are already committed to public shaming. That's obviously not enough. I don't know--but one thing I'm sure of is that if you tax shitty food like they taxed cigarettes, people will stop buying it.

Again, I'm not saying I'm comfortable with taxing it--but I do honestly believe that it would work. And if we have an obesity epidemic that's fueling the entire nation's health-care costs, then realistic solutions need to be discussed. For those suggesting taxing people based on BMI--that's a total pipe dream. It will NEVER happen and would probably be struck down by the SCOTUS. Australian here. We sort of have this. When our country wide Goods and Services Tax (Value Added Tax for the rest of the world) was implemented, due to the political horse trading the compromise was that necessities of life didn't incur the tax. Broadly speaking; medical goods/services, education, simple clothes and basic food (meats, fruit, vegetables etc) incur no tax. For example fresh potatoes won't incur any GST but frozen chips will.

Every now and then the "Fat Tax" argument comes up down here but as we sort of have it in reverse it doesn't get much momentum. This is before the pros/cons of different models are discussed.

As the principle has been established through the Excise system (extra taxes on tobacco and alcohol products), I think that it is a reasonable extension and option. However the libertarian in me is uncomfortable with social policy being achieved through a revenue based policy. That said, personal responsibility is failing and the already stressed medical system can only handle so many land whales. I'm not crazy about it but I think it could work as part of a wider approach to combating obesity.
